q: In a free-recall task with a 20-word list, words from the start of the list are recalled better than words from the middle. What is this advantage called?
options: Recency effect
Primacy effect
Von Restorff (isolation) effect
Spacing effect
explain: Better recall of early list items is the primacy effect, usually linked to extra rehearsal that moves those items into long-term memory.

q: One group recalls a 15-word list immediately; another counts backward for 30 seconds before recall. Which pattern best fits the two-store account of the serial position curve?
options: The recency effect shrinks or disappears in the delayed group, while primacy is largely unchanged
The primacy effect disappears in the delayed group, while recency is unchanged
Both primacy and recency become stronger after the delay
The delay has no effect because all items are already in long-term memory
explain: Recency is attributed to items still held in short-term memory, which a filled delay displaces; primacy depends on long-term storage and survives the delay.

q: In the Brown–Peterson task, why do participants count backward by threes after seeing a consonant trigram?
options: To strengthen the trigram through deeper semantic processing
To measure how fast participants can do arithmetic
To give a retrieval cue that matches the encoding context
To prevent rehearsal of the trigram during the retention interval
explain: The distractor task blocks rehearsal, so the experimenter can see how quickly unrehearsed information is lost from short-term memory.

q: In a simulated Brown–Peterson run, recall is high on trial 1 but drops across trials 2–5 when every trigram comes from the same category (all consonants). Recall recovers when trial 6 switches to digits. What best explains this?
options: Retroactive interference from later items erasing earlier ones
Pure time-based decay that resets when the category changes
Proactive interference from earlier similar items, followed by release from proactive interference
Fatigue that disappears when the stimuli become numbers
explain: Earlier similar items disrupt recall of new ones (proactive interference); changing the category removes that similarity and recall rebounds.

q: You want participants to remember the word TIGER as well as possible in a levels-of-processing study. Which orienting question should you pair with it?
options: Is the word printed in capital letters?
Is it an animal that could be dangerous in a forest?
Does the word rhyme with "fiber"?
How many vowels does the word contain?
explain: Questions about meaning (semantic processing) produce deeper processing and better later recall than questions about appearance or sound.

q: Which is the strongest criticism of the original levels-of-processing framework?
options: "Depth" was not measured independently, so defining deep processing by better recall risks circular reasoning
It predicts that shallow processing should give better recall than deep processing
It was never tested in experiments with words
It denies that rehearsal exists at all
explain: Without an independent index of depth, saying "deep processing leads to good memory" and "good memory shows deep processing" becomes circular.

q: Participants hear: bed, rest, awake, tired, dream, snooze, blanket, doze, slumber, nap. Which word, never presented, are they most likely to falsely recall?
options: Pillow
Night
Yawn
Sleep
explain: In the DRM paradigm, every list word is associated with one unpresented critical lure (here "sleep"), which is often recalled or recognised.

q: What does the DRM paradigm show about false memories?
options: False memories occur only in people with memory disorders
False memories disappear when people are confident
False memories of related words can be produced reliably in the lab and may be reported with high confidence
False memories happen only after long delays of several months
explain: DRM creates false recall of semantically related lures in ordinary participants within minutes, and people are often confident about them.

q: In Loftus and Palmer (1974), which verb in the question "About how fast were the cars going when they ___ each other?" produced the highest mean speed estimate?
options: Collided (39.3 mph)
Smashed (40.8 mph)
Hit (34.0 mph)
Contacted (31.8 mph)
explain: The mean estimate was 40.8 mph for "smashed" versus 31.8 mph for "contacted", showing that question wording shifts reports.

q: One week after the film, 16 of 50 "smashed" participants (32%) said they saw broken glass, versus 7 of 50 "hit" participants (14%). What does this follow-up add to the speed-estimate finding?
options: It suggests the verb changed the stored memory of the event, not only the answer to the speed question
It proves that the "smashed" group had better eyesight
It shows that leading questions have no effect after a delay
It shows that the "hit" group forgot the whole film
explain: Reporting a related detail a week later suggests the leading verb altered the memory representation, not just a momentary response bias.

q: A simulated police station asks you to improve its lineup procedure to reduce mistaken identifications. Which change is best supported by eyewitness research?
options: Telling the witness the suspect has already been arrested and is in the lineup
Having the investigating officer, who knows the suspect, run the lineup
Giving confirming feedback ("Good, you chose our suspect") to boost confidence
A double-blind lineup with an instruction that the culprit may or may not be present
explain: Double-blind administration and an unbiased "may not be present" instruction reduce cues and pressure that inflate false identifications.

q: In the Baddeley and Hitch working memory model, which component holds and manipulates visual and spatial information?
options: Phonological loop
Central executive
Visuospatial sketchpad
Long-term store
explain: The visuospatial sketchpad handles visual and spatial material; the phonological loop handles speech-based material.

q: Repeating "the, the, the" aloud impairs recall of a spoken digit list but barely affects a mental-rotation task. What does this dual-task pattern suggest?
options: Working memory is a single, unitary store
Verbal and visuospatial material use partly separate working-memory components
Articulatory suppression improves visual memory
Mental rotation depends mainly on the phonological loop
explain: Interference within the verbal domain but not across domains supports separate subsystems (phonological loop versus visuospatial sketchpad).

q: In a 2-back task the letters appear in this order: K, R, K, T, R, T, T. On which positions should the participant respond "target"?
options: 3rd and 6th
3rd and 7th
6th and 7th
5th and 6th
explain: A target matches the letter two positions back: position 3 (K = K at 1) and position 6 (T = T at 4); position 7 (T) is compared with position 5 (R).

q: In a simulated n-back study, accuracy falls and response times rise as n increases from 1 to 3. Which conclusion is best?
options: Higher n mainly tests long-term semantic memory
Participants become less motivated only on 3-back trials
The stimuli become physically harder to see as n increases
Higher n places greater load on continuous updating of working memory
explain: Larger n requires holding and updating more items at once, so performance costs index working-memory load.

q: Cowan (2001) argued for a central capacity limit in short-term memory of about how many chunks?
options: About seven chunks
About two chunks
About four chunks (roughly 3–5)
About twelve chunks
explain: Cowan reviewed evidence for a limit averaging about four chunks, smaller than Miller's (1956) classic "about seven".

q: A student must hold the string F B I C I A N A S A B B C. If they recognise four familiar acronyms, about how many chunks are they holding?
options: 13 chunks, far beyond any estimated limit
4 chunks, within Cowan's estimated limit
7 chunks, exactly at Miller's limit
1 chunk, because letters cannot be chunked
explain: FBI, CIA, NASA and BBC form four meaningful units, so 13 letters become four chunks, close to Cowan's limit of about four.

q: A student wants to memorise ten brain structures in order using the method of loci in the Memory Palace. What should they do?
options: Place a vivid image of each structure at successive locations on a familiar route, then mentally walk the route at recall
Repeat the list aloud ten times without any imagery
Write each term once and reread the list the night before
Group the terms alphabetically and memorise the first letters only
explain: The method of loci links each item to an ordered, well-known location; mentally retracing the route gives cues in the correct order.

q: Students who study and are tested in the same room tend to recall more than students tested in a different room. Which principle explains this?
options: Proactive interference from earlier learning
The primacy effect
Decay of short-term memory traces
Encoding specificity: retrieval is better when retrieval cues match the encoding context
explain: Context present during encoding becomes part of the memory trace, so reinstating it provides helpful retrieval cues.

q: Which claim about memory is best supported by research on misinformation and false memory?
options: Memories are stored like exact video recordings
Forgetting is caused only by time-based decay
Memory is reconstructive, so a confident report can still be inaccurate
Memories recovered under hypnosis are reliably accurate
explain: Misinformation and DRM studies show that memories are rebuilt at retrieval and can be distorted; confidence does not guarantee accuracy.

q: A forensic student argues that Loftus and Palmer's film-based findings may not fully generalise to real eyewitnesses. Which point best supports that critique?
options: The study used too many different verbs
Lab participants watched a short film with no real stakes, unlike witnesses to a real, emotional event
Speed estimates cannot be measured in miles per hour
The study included a control group
explain: Low ecological validity (a filmed event, no consequences) is the main limit on generalising to real crimes, though field work supports the broad conclusion.

q: After several news reports of a plane crash, a person rates flying as more dangerous than driving. Which heuristic best explains this judgement?
options: Anchoring and adjustment
Representativeness heuristic
Availability heuristic
Affect-free base-rate reasoning
explain: Vivid, recent examples come to mind easily, so people overestimate how common or likely the event is.

q: Sana studied philosophy, is outspoken and cares about social justice. Which is more probable: (A) Sana is a bank teller, or (B) Sana is a bank teller and active in a social-justice group?
options: B is more probable, because the description fits an activist
A is more probable, because a conjunction cannot be more likely than one of its parts
A and B are equally probable
They cannot be compared without knowing her salary
explain: Choosing B is the conjunction fallacy driven by representativeness; P(teller and activist) can never exceed P(teller).

q: A simulated screening test detects a condition in 90% of people who have it, and gives a false positive in 9% of people who do not. Only 1% of the population has the condition. If someone tests positive, roughly what is the chance they have it?
options: About 9%
About 90%
About 50%
About 1%
explain: Per 1,000 people: 9 true positives (90% of 10) and about 89 false positives (9% of 990), so 9/98 ≈ 9%; ignoring the 1% base rate inflates the estimate.

q: Two groups choose between a sure option and a risky option with identical expected outcomes. One group reads "200 of 600 people will be saved"; the other reads "400 of 600 people will die". What does prospect theory predict?
options: The "saved" (gain) frame makes the risky option more attractive
Both frames produce the same choices because the outcomes are identical
Both groups will always pick the sure option
The "die" (loss) frame makes the risky option more attractive
explain: People tend to be risk-averse for gains and risk-seeking for losses, so the same outcome framed as a loss shifts choices toward the gamble.

q: One group is asked whether the Indus River is longer or shorter than 500 km; another group is asked about 5,000 km. Both then estimate the actual length. What result does anchoring predict?
options: Both groups give the same average estimate
The 500 km group gives higher estimates
The 5,000 km group gives higher estimates on average than the 500 km group
Estimates become more accurate in the group with the higher number
explain: An arbitrary starting value pulls later estimates toward it, because adjustment away from the anchor is usually insufficient.

q: Four cards show E, K, 4 and 7. Each has a letter on one side and a number on the other. Rule: "If a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other." Which cards must you turn over to test the rule?
options: E and 4
E and 7
E only
E, 4 and 7
explain: Only E (could hide an odd number) and 7 (could hide a vowel) can falsify the rule; the 4 cannot break it whatever is on its back.

q: Most people choose E and 4 in the abstract Wason task. What does choosing the 4 card reveal about their reasoning?
options: A tendency to seek confirming rather than falsifying evidence
A correct understanding of modus tollens
A memory failure for the rule
A perceptual error in reading the cards
explain: The 4 can only confirm, never disconfirm, the rule; selecting it reflects confirmation or matching bias rather than a test of falsification.

q: Given a candle, a box of tacks and matches, many people fail to use the empty box as a shelf for the candle. What is this obstacle called?
options: Insight
Means–ends analysis
Algorithmic search
Functional fixedness
explain: Functional fixedness is difficulty seeing an object in a new use because we see it only in its usual function (a box as a container).

q: On the Hanoi bench the minimum number of moves for n discs is 2ⁿ − 1. What is the minimum for 4 discs?
explain: 2⁴ − 1 = 16 − 1 = 15 moves; 31 would be the minimum for 5 discs.

q: A solver breaks a Tower of Hanoi problem into sub-goals, each reducing the difference between the current state and the goal. Which strategy is this?
options: Trial and error
Means–ends analysis
Functional fixedness
Availability heuristic
explain: Means–ends analysis sets sub-goals that progressively reduce the gap between current and goal states.

q: In mental-rotation tasks, the time to decide whether two 3D shapes are the same rises steadily as the angle between them increases. What does this pattern suggest?
options: People rotate an analogue mental image, so larger angles take longer
People compare lists of verbal features that do not depend on angle
Larger angles make the shapes physically smaller
Response time depends only on how many cubes the shape has
explain: A roughly linear rise in time with angle is taken as evidence that mental images are transformed gradually, like physical rotation.

q: Which result on the rotation bench would most clearly challenge the analogue-rotation account?
options: Response times increase with angle
Mirror-image pairs take time to reject
Accuracy is high at small angles
Response times are the same at 0°, 60°, 120° and 180°
explain: The analogue account predicts time increases with angle; flat response times across angles would contradict it.

q: Spearman proposed a general factor, g. What observation was it mainly meant to explain?
options: Some people excel at music but not mathematics
Intelligence scores rise across generations
Scores on different mental tests tend to correlate positively with one another
Intelligence cannot be measured by tests
explain: The "positive manifold" of correlations among diverse tests led Spearman to propose a shared general ability.

q: Which task mainly draws on crystallised rather than fluid intelligence?
options: Solving a novel matrix-style pattern puzzle
Defining the meaning of uncommon vocabulary words
Finding the rule in an unfamiliar number series
Working out a new route through an unfamiliar maze
explain: Crystallised intelligence is accumulated knowledge such as vocabulary; fluid intelligence is reasoning with novel problems.

q: A student is skilled at reading classmates' moods and resolving group conflicts. In Gardner's framework, which intelligence does this best reflect?
options: Interpersonal
Intrapersonal
Logical–mathematical
Naturalistic
explain: Interpersonal intelligence concerns understanding others; intrapersonal concerns understanding oneself.

q: Which is the strongest scientific criticism of Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences?
options: It includes too few kinds of ability to be useful
It is identical to Spearman's g theory
It was based only on reaction-time data
There is limited psychometric evidence that the proposed intelligences are independent abilities
explain: Critics note that many "intelligences" correlate with g or look like talents, and that independent measures are scarce.

q: What does the Flynn effect refer to, and what is one practical consequence?
options: Intelligence declines steadily after age 20, so adults need separate tests
Twins have identical IQ scores, so heritability is 100%
Average raw scores on intelligence tests rose across generations, so tests need periodic re-norming
IQ scores are fixed at birth, so norms never change
explain: Rising raw-score performance over decades means old norms overstate a person's standing, so tests must be re-standardised.

q: Which explanation of the Flynn effect is least plausible?
options: Better nutrition and health
Genetic change in the population over a few generations
More schooling and familiarity with abstract tasks
Smaller families and richer learning environments
explain: The gains happened too quickly to be explained by genetic change; environmental explanations fit the time scale.

q: A deviation IQ scale has mean 100 and SD 15. What z-score corresponds to an IQ of 130?
explain: z = (130 − 100) / 15 = 2.0, i.e., two standard deviations above the mean.

q: Two groups differ in mean scores on a simulated aptitude test, but the test predicts later grades equally well in both groups (same regression line). What follows?
options: The test is necessarily biased because the means differ
The test has zero validity for both groups
One group must have been given different items
The mean difference alone does not show predictive bias against either group
explain: Predictive bias is judged by whether prediction differs by group; a mean difference by itself is not proof of test bias, though its causes still need study.

q: Which statement best describes the "weak" form of the linguistic relativity (Sapir–Whorf) hypothesis?
options: Language completely determines what people can think
Thought has no relation to language at all
Language can influence how people perceive or remember some things
All languages share the same words for colours
explain: The weak form claims influence, which has some support; the strong determinist form is largely rejected.

q: What is the correct order of Piaget's stages of cognitive development?
options: Preoperational, sensorimotor, formal operational, concrete operational
Sensorimotor, concrete operational, preoperational, formal operational
Formal operational, concrete operational, preoperational, sensorimotor
Sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational
explain: Piaget described a fixed sequence from sensorimotor (infancy) to formal operational (adolescence onward).

q: In the suite, juice is poured from a short wide glass into a tall thin glass while a child watches. The child says the tall glass now has more. Which stage best fits this answer?
options: Concrete operational
Formal operational
Preoperational
Sensorimotor
explain: Failing conservation of liquid quantity is typical of the preoperational stage; it is usually mastered in concrete operations.

q: According to Piaget, which two limitations best explain why a child fails the liquid-conservation task?
options: Lack of object permanence and stranger anxiety
Centration on one dimension (height) and lack of reversibility
Abstract hypothetical reasoning and egocentric speech
Poor vision and short attention span
explain: The child centres on height and cannot mentally reverse the pouring, so does not see that quantity is unchanged.

q: An infant finds a toy under cloth A several times. The toy is then hidden under cloth B while the infant watches, but the infant searches under A again. What is this, and to which stage does Piaget link it?
options: The A-not-B error, during the sensorimotor stage
A conservation error, during the preoperational stage
A false-belief error, during the concrete operational stage
Centration, during the formal operational stage
explain: Piaget saw the A-not-B error as a sign of incomplete object permanence late in the sensorimotor stage.

q: Which alternative explanation most directly challenges Piaget's view that the A-not-B error shows a weak object concept?
options: Infants cannot see the cloths clearly
Infants prefer cloth A because of its colour
Infants forget the toy exists once it is out of sight for one second
Infants may know where the toy is but cannot inhibit a repeated reaching habit
explain: Motor perseveration and immature inhibitory control (linked to prefrontal development) can produce the error even when the location is known.

q: What does "object permanence" mean in Piaget's theory?
options: Understanding that quantity stays the same when shape changes
Understanding that others can hold false beliefs
Understanding that objects continue to exist when out of sight
Understanding that rules can be changed by agreement
explain: Object permanence is the knowledge that objects exist independently of one's perception of them.

q: Ali puts a marble in the basket and leaves. While he is away, Zara moves it to the box. Ali returns. A child who passes the false-belief test will say Ali looks first where?
options: In the box
In the basket
In both places at once
Nowhere, because Ali knows it moved
explain: Passing requires seeing that Ali holds a false belief (basket) different from reality (box).

q: A young child answers "in the box" on the false-belief task. What is the best interpretation?
options: The child does not yet represent that another person's belief can differ from reality
The child has an attachment problem
The child lacks object permanence
The child cannot conserve number
explain: Answering with the true location suggests the child is reporting reality rather than the other person's belief, i.e., an immature theory of mind.

q: In the "unexpected contents" task, a child sees a sweets tube, learns it holds pencils, and is asked what a friend will think is inside. What is being measured?
options: Conservation of volume
Attachment security
Moral reasoning level
Understanding of false belief (theory of mind)
explain: The task tests whether the child can attribute to others (and to their own past self) a belief that differs from what they now know.

q: What is the main purpose of the Strange Situation procedure?
options: To measure an infant's IQ
To test conservation of number
To assess infant–caregiver attachment from behaviour across brief separations and reunions
To diagnose developmental disorders
explain: Coders focus especially on how the infant responds to the caregiver at reunion after separations involving a stranger.

q: In a simulated Strange Situation, the infant shows little distress at separation and turns away from the caregiver at reunion. Which classification fits best?
options: Secure
Insecure-avoidant
Insecure-resistant (ambivalent)
No classification is possible from reunion behaviour
explain: Avoiding or ignoring the caregiver at reunion is the key marker of the avoidant pattern.

q: A simulated infant cries when the caregiver leaves, seeks contact at reunion, is soothed quickly and returns to play. Which classification fits best?
options: Secure
Insecure-avoidant
Insecure-resistant (ambivalent)
Disorganised
explain: Using the caregiver as a secure base and being comforted on reunion are the hallmarks of secure attachment.

q: A simulated infant is very distressed at separation; at reunion they reach for the caregiver but also push away angrily and stay hard to soothe. Which classification fits best?
options: Secure
Insecure-avoidant
Securely detached
Insecure-resistant (ambivalent)
explain: Mixing contact-seeking with angry resistance and slow soothing marks the resistant (ambivalent) pattern.

q: Which is the strongest cultural critique of using the Strange Situation unchanged in, for example, extended-family households in Pakistan?
options: The procedure is too long for any infant to complete
Attachment cannot be observed in behaviour at all
Separation from a caregiver and meeting strangers may mean something different where infants are rarely left alone, so behaviour may be misread
Only fathers can take part in the procedure
explain: The procedure's meaning depends on everyday caregiving norms, so classifications may not be equivalent across cultures.

q: According to Erikson, what is the main psychosocial challenge of adolescence?
options: Trust versus mistrust
Identity versus role confusion
Generativity versus stagnation
Integrity versus despair
explain: Adolescents work to build a coherent sense of who they are; failure leaves role confusion.

q: A 45-year-old simulated lecturer spends time mentoring junior staff and worries about what she will leave behind. Which Eriksonian stage is most relevant?
options: Generativity versus stagnation
Intimacy versus isolation
Industry versus inferiority
Integrity versus despair
explain: Middle adulthood centres on contributing to the next generation (generativity).

q: Asked about the Heinz dilemma, a student says: "He should steal the drug because human life is a universal value that outweighs property law." Which level of moral reasoning is this?
options: Conventional
Preconventional
Pre-moral
Postconventional
explain: Appealing to universal ethical principles above specific laws is typical of postconventional reasoning.

q: A child says: "Heinz should not steal because he would be put in jail." Which level of moral reasoning does this reflect?
options: Conventional
Postconventional
Preconventional
Formal operational
explain: Reasoning based on avoiding punishment is preconventional; Kohlberg scored the reasoning, not the yes/no answer.

q: Which is a well-known criticism of Kohlberg's theory?
options: It ignores moral reasoning entirely and studies only behaviour
It may underweight care-based moral reasoning and reflect Western, individualist values
It proposes too many stages to test
It applies only to infants
explain: Gilligan argued for a care orientation, and cross-cultural researchers questioned whether the top stages are universal; reasoning also may not predict behaviour.

q: A study compares memory scores of 20-, 45- and 70-year-olds tested once in 2026. The oldest group scores lowest. Why can't we conclude that ageing alone caused the difference?
options: Age is confounded with cohort (generation) effects in a cross-sectional design
Longitudinal designs always find no age differences
Memory cannot be measured in older adults
The sample included too many age groups
explain: Groups differ in education and life experience as well as age; following the same people over time (longitudinal or sequential designs) helps separate these.

q: A teacher gives a child hints on a puzzle the child cannot yet solve alone, then gradually withdraws the hints as the child improves. Which concept does this illustrate?
options: Centration
Assimilation without accommodation
Object permanence
Scaffolding within the zone of proximal development
explain: Vygotsky's ZPD is what a learner can do with help; scaffolding is support that is faded as competence grows.

q: Which statement matches the James–Lange theory of emotion?
options: We feel afraid because we notice our body trembling and heart racing
Bodily arousal and the feeling of fear occur at the same time and independently
Emotion requires arousal plus a cognitive label for that arousal
Emotions are produced only by the cortex without bodily change
explain: James–Lange says the felt emotion is the perception of bodily changes that follow the stimulus.

q: Which statement matches the Cannon–Bard theory?
options: Feelings follow from perceiving bodily change
Arousal is labelled by searching the situation for a cause
Facial muscles alone cause the feeling of emotion
Bodily arousal and the subjective feeling arise at the same time, both triggered via the thalamus
explain: Cannon and Bard argued that arousal and feeling are simultaneous and independent rather than sequential.

q: A student drinks strong coffee, then meets someone at a wedding and interprets the racing heart as attraction. Which theory best explains this?
options: James–Lange theory
Cannon–Bard theory
Schachter–Singer two-factor theory (misattribution of arousal)
Drive-reduction theory
explain: Two-factor theory says emotion is arousal plus a cognitive label; caffeine-based arousal is here wrongly attributed to the person.

q: Which observation most directly challenges the James–Lange theory?
options: People report emotions in response to events
Quite different emotions can be accompanied by similar patterns of autonomic arousal
The heart rate rises during fear
Emotions can be described in words
explain: Cannon argued that if arousal patterns are similar across emotions, bodily change alone cannot tell us which emotion we feel.

q: In Lazarus's appraisal model of stress, what is primary appraisal?
options: Judging whether an event is relevant and threatening, harmful or challenging
Judging whether one has the resources to cope
The hormonal response of the adrenal glands
Re-evaluating the situation after coping
explain: Primary appraisal asks "Is this a problem for me?"; secondary appraisal asks "Can I cope with it?".

q: In the FACS face lab you combine AU6 (cheek raiser) with AU12 (lip corner puller). Which expression results?
options: A frown of anger
An expression of disgust
A look of surprise
A Duchenne (felt) smile
explain: AU12 pulls the lip corners up; adding AU6 raises the cheeks and crinkles the eye corners, the classic Duchenne smile.

q: You set AU1 (inner brow raiser), AU2 (outer brow raiser) and AU26 (jaw drop). Which prototypical expression is this closest to?
options: Sadness
Anger
Surprise
Disgust
explain: Raised brows with a dropped jaw form the typical surprise configuration.

q: A coder sees AU12 with no AU6 on a simulated face. What is the most defensible conclusion?
options: The person is certainly lying
The lip corners are pulled up without cheek raising; any emotional meaning, such as a polite smile, is an inference beyond the coding
The person is certainly happy
FACS cannot code smiles
explain: FACS describes observable muscle movements; linking a pattern to an inner state is a separate interpretive step.

q: What is the Facial Action Coding System (FACS)?
options: An anatomically based system for coding visible facial muscle movements as action units
A questionnaire that measures emotional intelligence
A brain-imaging method for locating emotions
A list of the six basic emotions with their causes
explain: FACS codes facial movements by the muscles that produce them, separating description from emotional interpretation.

q: Which sequence describes the HPA stress axis?
options: Pituitary releases cortisol → hypothalamus releases ACTH → adrenal medulla releases CRH
Adrenal cortex releases CRH → hypothalamus releases cortisol → pituitary releases ACTH
Thyroid releases ACTH → pituitary releases CRH → adrenal cortex releases insulin
Hypothalamus releases CRH → pituitary releases ACTH → adrenal cortex releases cortisol
explain: CRH from the hypothalamus triggers ACTH from the pituitary, which triggers cortisol from the adrenal cortex.

q: In the HPA simulator you raise circulating cortisol. If negative feedback is working normally, what should happen next?
options: CRH and ACTH release should increase
Only adrenaline release should increase
CRH and ACTH release should decrease
Nothing, because cortisol does not act on the brain
explain: Cortisol acts on the hypothalamus and pituitary to dampen CRH and ACTH, which limits the stress response.

q: Which system produces the fastest bodily stress response, within seconds?
options: The HPA axis releasing cortisol
The sympathetic–adrenal–medullary (SAM) system releasing adrenaline
The immune system producing antibodies
The digestive system releasing insulin
explain: Sympathetic activation of the adrenal medulla is rapid; the hormonal HPA cascade is slower.

q: What is the order of stages in Selye's general adaptation syndrome?
options: Alarm, resistance, exhaustion
Resistance, alarm, exhaustion
Exhaustion, alarm, resistance
Alarm, exhaustion, recovery
explain: An initial alarm reaction is followed by resistance and, if stress continues, exhaustion.

q: Before exams, a simulated student makes a study timetable and asks a tutor for help with weak topics. Which coping style is this?
options: Emotion-focused coping
Avoidance coping
Denial
Problem-focused coping
explain: Problem-focused coping acts on the stressor itself; emotion-focused coping manages the feelings it causes.

q: A simulated client is waiting several weeks for medical test results and can do nothing to change them. Which coping approach is usually more adaptive here?
options: Problem-focused attempts to change the test result
Constantly checking for results every hour
Emotion-focused strategies such as relaxation, acceptance and seeking support
Avoiding all thoughts and people until the result arrives
explain: When a stressor is uncontrollable, managing emotional responses fits the situation better than trying to change the stressor.

q: A simulated client has frequent tension headaches. Which factor is a psychological component in the biopsychosocial model?
options: A family history of migraine
Catastrophic thoughts about what the pain means
Noise and long shifts at work
Support from family members
explain: Thoughts and beliefs are psychological; family history is biological, while work conditions and family support are social or environmental.

q: Using the inverted-U curve as an illustrative model, at what level of arousal would you expect best performance on a complex, unfamiliar task?
options: A moderate level, lower than the best level for a simple, well-practised task
The highest possible level
The lowest possible level
Arousal level makes no difference to performance
explain: The illustrative model predicts a moderate optimum that is lower for harder tasks; it is a teaching heuristic, not a precise law.

q: A coaching app claims the Yerkes–Dodson law gives the exact arousal level each athlete needs. How should a psychology student judge this claim?
options: Accept it, because the law has a fixed numeric optimum for everyone
Reject any link between arousal and performance
Accept it, because laws in psychology are never revised
Treat the inverted-U as an illustrative idea, not a precise law that sets exact optimal levels
explain: The inverted-U is useful for teaching but does not give exact, individual optima; precise claims need direct evidence.

q: Students who already enjoyed reading are paid for each book; when payments stop, they read less than before. Which concept explains this?
options: Drive reduction
Social facilitation
The overjustification effect
Learned helplessness
explain: Expected external rewards can shift the perceived reason for an enjoyed activity, undermining intrinsic motivation.

q: Self-determination theory proposes three basic psychological needs. Which list is correct?
options: Safety, esteem, self-actualisation
Autonomy, competence, relatedness
Achievement, power, affiliation
Hunger, thirst, sleep
explain: SDT holds that supporting autonomy, competence and relatedness fosters intrinsic motivation and well-being.

q: A survey finds that students reporting more daily hassles also report more colds. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Hassles and colds are associated, but the survey alone cannot show that hassles cause colds
Daily hassles definitely cause colds
Colds definitely cause daily hassles
There is no relationship because surveys are unreliable
explain: A correlation could reflect causation in either direction or a third variable (e.g., poor sleep); experiments or longitudinal designs are needed.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the Big Five personality domains?
options: Openness to experience
Psychoticism
Conscientiousness
Agreeableness
explain: The Big Five are openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism; psychoticism belongs to Eysenck's model.

q: Why can ZEHN show International Personality Item Pool (IPIP) items to learners?
options: IPIP items are in the public domain and may be freely copied, edited and translated
IPIP items are licensed only for clinical diagnosis
IPIP is a copyrighted commercial test with a free trial
IPIP items are taken from the MMPI
explain: The IPIP offers over 3,000 public-domain items and over 250 scales; any self-report use in ZEHN is for learning only, not diagnosis.

q: On a 1–5 agreement scale, a respondent answers 2 to a reverse-keyed item. What is the scored value?
explain: Reverse-scoring on a 1–5 scale uses 6 − response, so 6 − 2 = 4.

q: A simulated participant is described as organised, dependable, careful and goal-directed. Which Big Five domain is highest?
options: Extraversion
Openness to experience
Conscientiousness
Agreeableness
explain: Organisation, dependability and goal-directed persistence are core facets of conscientiousness.

q: What does Bandura's reciprocal determinism propose?
options: Personality is fixed by genes and unaffected by situations
Behaviour, personal factors and the environment influence each other
Behaviour is controlled only by reinforcement from the environment
Unconscious conflicts determine all behaviour
explain: Reciprocal determinism describes a three-way interaction rather than one-way causation.

q: A simulated student is reliably honest with family but often copies answers in exams. How would a social-cognitive (Mischel-style) theorist interpret this?
options: Behaviour shows stable if–then patterns tied to situations, rather than one global trait level
The student has no personality
This proves broad traits fully predict single behaviours
The data must be a measurement error
explain: Mischel argued that people show consistent situation–behaviour profiles ("if–then signatures"), which single trait scores can miss.

q: What does test–retest reliability assess?
options: Agreement between two different raters
Correlation among items within one administration
Whether the test measures what it claims to measure
Consistency of scores when the same test is given to the same people at two times
explain: Test–retest reliability is the stability of scores across time.

q: Two trainee clinicians independently rate the same recorded simulated interviews. Which reliability are you estimating?
options: Test–retest reliability
Parallel-forms reliability
Inter-rater reliability
Split-half reliability
explain: Agreement between independent raters scoring the same material is inter-rater reliability.

q: A 10-item scale has reliability r = .60. Using the Spearman–Brown formula, what is the predicted reliability if you double its length with similar items (k = 2)?
A test has SD = 15 and reliability r = .91. What is the standard error of measurement (SEM)?
A simulated client scores 104 on a test with SEM = 4.5. Which is the best approximate 95% band for the true score?
options: About 99.5 to 108.5
Exactly 104
About 86 to 122
About 95 to 113
explain: The 95% band is about ±1.96 × SEM = ±8.8, giving roughly 95–113; ±1 SEM gives only about a 68% band.

q: A 4-item scale has a sum of item variances of 4 and a total-score variance of 10. What is Cronbach's α?
A 40-item scale built in the Test-Construction Studio has α = .95. Which caution is most appropriate?
options: α = .95 proves the scale is valid
High α can partly reflect many or redundant items and does not by itself prove the scale is unidimensional
α = .95 means 95% of the variance is the construct of interest
α should always be above .99 for research use
explain: Alpha rises with test length and item redundancy; dimensionality and validity need separate evidence such as factor analysis.

q: A new anxiety scale correlates strongly with an established anxiety measure. Which kind of validity evidence is this?
options: Convergent validity (construct validity)
Discriminant validity
Face validity
Test–retest reliability
explain: Convergent evidence shows that a measure relates as expected to other measures of the same construct.

q: Scores on a simulated selection test taken at hiring correlate with supervisor ratings one year later. What kind of validity is this?
options: Concurrent validity
Content validity
Face validity
Predictive (criterion-related) validity
explain: Criterion data collected later than the test gives predictive validity; collected at the same time it would be concurrent.

q: A new "grit" scale correlates r = .90 with an existing conscientiousness scale. Which problem does this raise?
options: Strong discriminant validity
Low internal consistency
Weak discriminant validity: the new scale may not measure anything distinct
Poor inter-rater reliability
explain: A very high correlation with a different construct suggests the scale may be a new name for an old construct (a "jangle" problem).

q: T-scores have mean 50 and SD 10. What T-score corresponds to z = +1.5?
Why does a test used with university students in Sindh ideally need norms from a comparable local sample?
options: A score is interpreted against the norm group, so an unrepresentative group can distort percentiles and conclusions
Local norms make a test more reliable automatically
Norms are needed only for projective tests
Without local norms a test cannot be scored at all
explain: Norm-referenced interpretation is only as good as the match between the norm sample and the people tested.

q: Which is the strongest psychometric criticism of projective techniques such as inkblot or picture-story methods?
options: They have too many multiple-choice items
They always use numbers instead of interpretations
They are too short to be scored
Scoring is often subjective, and evidence for inter-rater reliability and incremental validity is mixed
explain: Concerns centre on rater-dependent scoring, inconsistent norms and limited evidence that they add predictive value beyond simpler measures. ZEHN shows no real plates or cards.

q: Many students rate a generic personality description ("You sometimes doubt your decisions") as highly accurate for them. What does this imply about judging a personality test?
options: High accuracy ratings prove the test is valid
Students cannot judge their own personality at all
Feeling that feedback is accurate is weak evidence of validity, because vague statements fit almost anyone
Generic descriptions are a form of reliability evidence
explain: The Barnum (Forer) effect shows that acceptance of feedback does not establish that a test measures anything specific.

q: A 5-item scale has low internal consistency. Which change is most likely to raise it?
options: Removing the reverse-keyed instructions
Adding more good items that measure the same construct
Shortening it to 3 items
Giving it to a smaller sample
explain: As Spearman–Brown shows, adding parallel items that tap the same construct increases reliability.

q: A student publicly agrees with friends' opinion of a film to fit in, while privately disagreeing. Which type of conformity is this?
options: Informational conformity
Internalisation
Normative conformity
Obedience
explain: Normative influence comes from wanting acceptance, so public compliance may not match private belief.

q: A new student unsure of the referencing style copies how classmates format citations, believing they know the correct rule. Which influence is this?
options: Normative influence
Informational influence
Obedience to authority
Social loafing
explain: Informational influence occurs when we use others as a source of accurate information in an ambiguous situation.

q: In the Asch-style line room, which change would most likely reduce conformity on critical trials?
options: One confederate breaks ranks and gives the correct answer
The group is made larger
Answers are given aloud rather than in writing
The confederates all wear the same uniform
explain: A single dissenting ally breaks unanimity and reduces pressure to conform; private responding also tends to reduce conformity.

q: In Darley and Latané's (1968) seizure study, about what proportion of participants who believed they were alone reported the emergency before the end of the fit, compared with those who believed four others could hear?
options: 31% alone versus 85% with four others
50% in both conditions
100% alone versus 0% with four others
85% alone versus 31% with four others
explain: Helping before the end of the fit fell from 85% (alone) to 31% (four others present).

q: Why did reporting drop so sharply when participants believed others also heard the seizure?
options: Participants in larger groups could not hear the victim
Larger groups contained less helpful personality types
Diffusion of responsibility: each person felt less personal duty to act
The victim asked only the solo participants for help
explain: With others present, responsibility is spread across people, so each is less likely to act.

q: You collapse at a busy chai dhaba in the Mohalla simulation. Based on bystander research, what is the best way to get help?
options: Call out generally "Somebody help!" to the whole crowd
Point to one specific person and give a specific task, such as "You in the blue shirt, call an ambulance"
Wait quietly so as not to alarm people
Ask the crowd to vote on what to do
explain: Singling out one person removes ambiguity and diffusion of responsibility by making them personally responsible.

q: In Festinger and Carlsmith (1959), which group later rated the boring task as most enjoyable?
options: Those paid $1 to tell the next participant it was enjoyable
Those paid $20
The control group who told no one anything
All groups gave the same rating
explain: Mean enjoyment ratings were +1.35 for the $1 group, −0.05 for $20 and −0.45 for controls.

q: Why does dissonance theory predict that the $1 group, not the $20 group, changed their attitude?
options: $1 participants were more honest people
The $20 group did not actually tell the lie
$1 rewards are reinforcing, so the task became enjoyable through conditioning
$1 was insufficient justification for lying, so they reduced dissonance by deciding the task was enjoyable
explain: Large payment justified the lie; small payment did not, so the inconsistency was resolved by changing the private attitude.

q: A simulated smoker who knows the health risks says, "My grandfather smoked and lived a long life." What is this?
options: The fundamental attribution error
Informational conformity
Reducing dissonance by adding a consonant cognition
Social facilitation
explain: Rather than quitting, the person adds a belief that makes smoking seem less inconsistent with wanting good health.

q: A driver cuts into traffic. An observer thinks, "What a rude person," without considering that the driver might be rushing to hospital. Which bias is shown?
options: Self-serving bias
Fundamental attribution error
False consensus effect
Hindsight bias
explain: The FAE overweights dispositional explanations for others' behaviour and underweights situational ones.

q: What does cross-cultural research suggest about the fundamental attribution error?
options: It tends to be weaker where people habitually attend to social context, as in many collectivist settings
It is identical in strength in every culture
It occurs only in collectivist cultures
It has never been studied outside one country
explain: People from more collectivist backgrounds often give greater weight to situational causes, though the bias is not absent.

q: Payoffs: both cooperate = 3 each; both defect = 1 each; if one defects and the other cooperates, the defector gets 5 and the cooperator 0. In a one-shot game, what is each player's dominant strategy?
options: Cooperate
Alternate randomly
There is no dominant strategy
Defect
explain: Whatever the other does, defecting pays more (5 > 3 and 1 > 0), yet mutual defection (1, 1) is worse for both than mutual cooperation (3, 3).

q: In repeated rounds of the dilemma, a player uses tit-for-tat. Why does this strategy tend to sustain cooperation?
options: It always defects, so partners give up
It cooperates no matter what the partner does
It starts by cooperating, punishes defection once, and forgives as soon as the partner cooperates again
It chooses at random so partners cannot predict it
explain: Tit-for-tat is nice, retaliatory, forgiving and clear, which makes cooperation the best reply for a partner.

q: In Milgram's 1963 baseline study, how many of the 40 participants continued to the maximum 450-volt level?
explain: Twenty-six of forty participants (65%) obeyed to 450 V, and none stopped before 300 V, in this single condition.

q: Judged by current research-ethics standards, which feature of Milgram's obedience procedure is most problematic?
options: Scripted prods pressured participants to continue, undermining their right to withdraw, and many showed strong distress
Participants were paid for their time
The study took place in a university building
Participants were adults
explain: Modern codes require a genuine right to withdraw and protection from serious distress; deception also requires careful justification and debriefing.

q: Le Texier (2019) analysed archives and interviewed 15 participants of the Stanford Prison Experiment. Which conclusion is best supported by this critique?
options: The study is now proven to have been run perfectly
Le Texier showed that the experiment never took place
The critique is accepted by everyone, including the original researchers
Claims that guard cruelty arose spontaneously from the situation are weakened, because guards received instructions and demand characteristics were present
explain: Le Texier reported guard instructions, demand characteristics and biased data collection; Zimbardo and Haney replied in 2020, so the debate is contested.

q: According to Zajonc, how does the presence of others affect performance?
options: It always improves performance
It always impairs performance
It increases arousal, which helps well-learned (dominant) responses but hurts new, difficult ones
It has no effect on arousal
explain: Arousal from an audience strengthens the dominant response, which is correct for easy tasks but often wrong for hard ones.

q: A simulated lab must hire research assistants. Which interviewing approach is best supported by selection research for predicting job performance?
options: An unstructured chat that changes with each candidate
A structured interview with job-related questions asked to every candidate and scored with rating anchors
Hiring the candidate the panel "clicks with" most
Choosing by handwriting analysis
explain: Standardised, job-related questions and scoring reduce bias and noise, so structured interviews predict performance better than unstructured ones.

q: Before designing a selection test for clinic receptionists, what should an I-O psychologist do first?
options: Conduct a job analysis to identify key tasks and the required knowledge, skills, abilities and other characteristics (KSAOs)
Buy the most popular personality test available
Copy the test another company uses for engineers
Select candidates first and analyse the job later
explain: Job analysis defines what the job requires, which is the basis for valid selection tools and criteria.

q: A simulated test selects 50% of applicants from Group A and 30% from Group B. Using the four-fifths (80%) rule of thumb, what is the conclusion?
options: The ratio is 1.67, so there is no concern
The ratio is .80, exactly at the threshold
Adverse impact cannot be judged from selection rates
The ratio is .60, below .80, which flags possible adverse impact for review
explain: Impact ratio = 30% / 50% = .60; below .80 signals a disparity that should be investigated, not automatic proof of bias.

q: A worker values the bonus offered and trusts that good performance will be rewarded, but believes extra effort cannot raise output because the equipment is broken. Under expectancy theory, why is motivation low?
options: Valence of the bonus is zero
Instrumentality (performance → reward) is low
Expectancy (effort → performance) is low
Goal difficulty is too low
explain: Expectancy theory multiplies expectancy, instrumentality and valence; if effort is not seen to raise performance, motivation falls even with a valued reward.

q: What does the diathesis–stress model propose?
options: Stress alone causes every psychological disorder
Genes alone determine whether a disorder develops
Disorders are caused only by childhood conflicts
Psychological problems arise from an interaction between a pre-existing vulnerability and environmental stress
explain: A diathesis (biological, psychological or social vulnerability) raises risk, and stressors may trigger difficulties in vulnerable people.

q: Simulated client "Bilal" (fictional) has a family history of low mood and develops persistent sadness after losing his job. His cousin, with a similar family history but no major stressors, does not. Which model best fits this simulated case?
options: Pure genetic determinism
Pure behaviourism
Diathesis–stress
Humanistic self-actualisation
explain: Shared vulnerability with different outcomes depending on stress is the core diathesis–stress pattern. This is a simulated case, not a diagnosis.

q: Which statement about the structure of DSM-5-TR is accurate?
options: It is published by the World Health Organization as one alphabetical list
It is published by the American Psychiatric Association and has three sections, with the diagnostic chapters in Section II
It contains no grouping of disorders into chapters
It replaced the ICD, which is no longer used
explain: DSM-5-TR groups disorders into chapters in Section II; Section III holds emerging measures and models. See DSM-5-TR for official criteria.

q: Which organisation publishes ICD-11?
options: The World Health Organization
The American Psychiatric Association
The American Psychological Association
The British Psychological Society
explain: ICD-11 is the WHO's International Classification of Diseases; mental, behavioural and neurodevelopmental disorders form one of its chapters.

q: A tutor argues that anxiety should be described as a score on a continuum rather than as present or absent. Which approach to classification is this?
options: Categorical
Projective
Idiographic only
Dimensional
explain: Dimensional approaches rate severity along continua; categorical approaches decide whether a diagnosis is present.

q: What is self-stigma?
options: When the public holds negative stereotypes about mental illness
When institutions have rules that disadvantage people with mental illness
When a person accepts negative public stereotypes about mental illness and applies them to themselves
When a clinician refuses to give a diagnosis
explain: Self-stigma is internalised public stigma; it can lower self-esteem and discourage help-seeking.

q: Which phrase follows person-first, less stigmatising language?
options: "A schizophrenic"
"A person living with schizophrenia"
"The mentally ill"
"A psycho"
explain: Person-first language describes a condition a person has rather than defining the person by it.

q: Which three core conditions did Carl Rogers propose for therapeutic change?
options: Empathy, unconditional positive regard and congruence
Interpretation, transference and free association
Exposure, reinforcement and extinction
Assessment, diagnosis and medication
explain: Rogers held that a genuine therapist who offers accurate empathy and unconditional positive regard enables client growth.

q: Simulated client: "I've been so tired I can't face my classes." Counsellor: "You're feeling worn out, and classes feel like too much right now." Which OARS skill is this?
options: Closed question
Affirmation
Summary
Reflection
explain: The counsellor mirrors the client's meaning and feeling back without asking or advising, which is a reflection.

q: A counsellor asks a simulated client, "Do you sleep eight hours a night?" How is this response classified?
options: Open question
Reflection
Closed question
Affirmation
explain: It can be answered "yes" or "no", so it is closed; OARS favours open questions to invite elaboration.

q: Which counsellor response is an open question?
options: "Did you go to class today?"
"What has been most difficult for you this term?"
"Are you feeling sad?"
"Is it your exams that worry you?"
explain: Open questions cannot be answered with one word and invite the client to tell their story.

q: A counsellor says to a simulated client, "It took real courage to come in today and talk about this." Which OARS skill is this?
options: Affirmation
Reflection
Summary
Closed question
explain: Affirmations recognise the client's strengths and efforts.

q: A simulated client admits failing an exam after skipping lectures. Which reply best shows unconditional positive regard?
options: "You only have yourself to blame for skipping lectures."
"Lots of students fail; it doesn't matter."
"If you promise to attend every lecture, then I can help you."
"You're disappointed in how this went, and I'm glad you're here to look at what happens next."
explain: UPR accepts the person without conditions, even if the behaviour is not endorsed; it avoids both blame and dismissing the concern.

q: Simulated client: a friend did not reply to a message (A); the client thought, "She must hate me" (B); the client felt sad and withdrew (C). Which element do CBT techniques mainly target for change?
options: A: the friend's unanswered message
C: feeling sad
B: the belief "She must hate me"
None, because events cause feelings directly
explain: In the ABC model, beliefs about events shape the consequences, so beliefs are examined and restructured.

q: A simulated client says, "If I get a B in this course, my whole career is ruined." Which cognitive distortion is this?
options: Mind reading
Catastrophising
Personalisation
Emotional reasoning
explain: Catastrophising predicts the worst possible outcome from a limited event.

q: A therapist asks a simulated client, "What evidence supports this thought, and what evidence goes against it?" What is the purpose of this technique?
options: Socratic questioning to test and restructure an unhelpful thought
Free association to reach unconscious material
Systematic desensitisation of a phobia
Reflecting feelings without challenging thoughts
explain: Weighing evidence for and against an automatic thought is a core CBT cognitive-restructuring step.

q: In more collectivist settings, such as many families in Pakistan, which pattern of help-seeking is commonly described?
options: People always seek professional help alone and in secret
Family plays no role in health decisions
Help-seeking is decided only by employers
Family members are often involved in decisions about whether and where to seek help
explain: Decisions may be made collectively, so culturally responsive services may involve family, with the client's consent.

q: A simulated client in Hyderabad attributes their distress partly to spiritual causes and also visits a faith healer. What is the most culturally competent response from the trainee counsellor?
options: Tell the client their beliefs are wrong before starting therapy
Refuse to work with the client until they stop seeing the healer
Respectfully explore the client's explanatory model and work collaboratively, while monitoring safety and referring when needed
Ignore the beliefs and follow a standard script
explain: Understanding the client's own explanation builds the alliance and fits care to their values, without giving up clinical responsibilities.

q: Why should a counsellor attend to bodily complaints, such as aches or fatigue, when a simulated client describes emotional distress?
options: Bodily complaints show that psychological factors are irrelevant
Distress is often expressed through bodily idioms shaped by culture, so physical complaints may carry emotional meaning
Physical symptoms always mean the client is exaggerating
Culture has no effect on how distress is expressed
explain: Cultures differ in how distress is voiced; DSM-5-TR discusses cultural concepts of distress for this reason.

q: What do the letters in Seligman's PERMA model stand for?
options: Positive emotion, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, Accomplishment
Personality, Emotion, Reasoning, Memory, Attention
Perception, Effort, Resilience, Motivation, Ability
Positive thinking, Exercise, Rest, Mindfulness, Activity
explain: PERMA lists five building blocks of well-being in Seligman's account.

q: After a brief gratitude and positive-mood exercise, simulated students generate more varied ideas in a problem-solving task. Which theory predicts this?
options: Selye's general adaptation syndrome
Festinger's cognitive dissonance theory
Drive-reduction theory
Fredrickson's broaden-and-build theory
explain: Broaden-and-build proposes that positive emotions widen attention and thinking and build resources over time.

q: The same 30 participants complete congruent and incongruent Stroop trials, and you compare their mean RTs. Which test fits this design?
options: Paired-samples (repeated-measures) t-test
Independent-samples t-test
Chi-square test of independence
Pearson correlation
explain: Each participant provides both scores, so the scores are paired.

q: Three separate groups of students are taught by three different methods, and you compare their mean exam scores. Which test fits?
options: Paired-samples t-test
Chi-square goodness-of-fit test
Three separate correlations
One-way between-subjects ANOVA
explain: Comparing means of three or more independent groups calls for a one-way ANOVA, which controls the error rate of multiple t-tests.

q: You count how many students in two departments prefer tea, coffee or neither. Which test asks whether preference is related to department?
options: Independent-samples t-test
One-way ANOVA
Chi-square test of independence
Paired-samples t-test
explain: Both variables are categorical and the data are counts, so a chi-square test of independence is appropriate (here df = (2 − 1)(3 − 1) = 2).

q: An independent-samples t-test compares two groups of 20 participants each. What are the degrees of freedom?
A one-way ANOVA has 3 groups with 10 participants each. Which degrees of freedom should be reported?
explain: df between = k − 1 = 2; df within = N − k = 30 − 3 = 27.

q: Group means are 105 and 100 with a pooled SD of 10. What is Cohen's d?
explain: d = (M₁ − M₂) / SD = 5 / 10 = 0.50, conventionally a "medium" effect.

q: What does a p-value represent in null hypothesis significance testing?
options: The probability that the null hypothesis is true
The probability that the result will replicate
The probability of results at least as extreme as those observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true
The size of the effect
explain: p is computed under the assumption that H₀ is true; it is not the probability of H₀ itself.

q: A student writes: "p = .03, so there is a 97% chance our hypothesis is true." What is wrong with this statement?
options: Nothing; this is the correct interpretation
p is computed assuming the null is true; it does not give the probability that any hypothesis is true
The p-value should have been multiplied by 100
p-values only apply to correlations
explain: Statements about the probability of hypotheses need other approaches (e.g., Bayesian); p only describes data under H₀.

topic: Type I and Type II errors
q: A simulated drug truly has no effect, but a study finds p < .05 and concludes that it works. Which error is this?
options: Type I error (false positive)
Type II error (false negative)
Sampling error with no decision error
Correct rejection
explain: Rejecting a true null hypothesis is a Type I error, whose long-run rate is set by α.

q: A study with 12 participants per group tests a real, moderate effect and finds p = .20. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The effect does not exist, proven by p > .05
A Type I error occurred
The alpha level was too strict at .20
Low statistical power produced a Type II error
explain: Small samples give low power to detect moderate effects, so failing to reject H₀ here is likely a false negative.

q: Which change increases the statistical power of a study, all else equal?
options: Lowering α from .05 to .01
Using a less reliable measure
Increasing the sample size
Studying a smaller true effect
explain: Power (1 − β) rises with larger samples, larger effects, more reliable measures and a less strict α.

q: A researcher checks the p-value after every 10 participants and stops as soon as p < .05. What is the problem?
options: It reduces the Type I error rate below 5%
Optional stopping inflates the Type I error rate above the nominal 5%
It is the recommended preregistered procedure
It only affects effect sizes, not p-values
explain: Repeated peeking without correction gives many chances for a false positive; sequential designs must be planned in advance.

q: A simulated lab measured six outcome variables but the paper reports only the one that reached p < .05. Which practice is this, and what best prevents it?
options: Selective reporting (a form of p-hacking); prevented by preregistering all outcomes and the analysis plan
Replication; prevented by using a larger α
Blinding; prevented by removing control groups
Random assignment; prevented by using a correlational design
explain: Reporting only significant outcomes hides the multiple tests run; preregistration makes all planned outcomes visible.

q: You run 5 planned comparisons and want a familywise α of .05. Using a Bonferroni correction, what α should each test use?
explain: Bonferroni divides α by the number of tests: .05 / 5 = .01.

q: What is preregistration?
options: Registering participants before they consent
Submitting a paper to two journals at once
Publicly recording hypotheses, design and analysis plan before collecting or analysing data
Registering a statistical software licence
explain: A time-stamped plan separates confirmatory from exploratory analyses and limits undisclosed flexibility.

q: In the Open Science Collaboration (2015) project replicating 100 studies, what share of original studies and of replications reported significant results?
options: 36% of originals versus 97% of replications
97% of originals versus 36% of replications
50% of originals versus 50% of replications
100% of originals versus 0% of replications
explain: Ninety-seven percent of the original studies were significant compared with 36% of the replications.

q: The OSC (2015) found replication effects were about half the magnitude of the original effects. Which interpretation is most defensible?
options: Published original effects were probably often inflated, for example by publication bias and low power
All of the original studies were fraudulent
Replications are always wrong, so original estimates should be trusted
Psychology findings never replicate
explain: Smaller replication effects fit a literature that favoured significant, possibly overestimated results; they do not imply fraud or total failure.

q: The ego-depletion registered replication report (23 labs, N = 2,141) found d = 0.04, 95% CI [−0.07, 0.15], while an earlier meta-analysis estimated d = 0.62. What is the best conclusion?
options: The RRR confirms a large ego-depletion effect
The two results agree because both are positive
The RRR is less trustworthy because it used many labs
The interval includes zero and excludes 0.62, so any effect is far smaller than the meta-analysis suggested
explain: A large, preregistered multi-lab study is strong evidence; its CI rules out an effect as large as d = 0.62 and is consistent with no effect.

q: Which result is reported in APA-7 style? (In the published version the statistic symbols would be italicised.)
explain: APA-7 gives df in parentheses, spaces around "=", an exact p without a leading zero, and an effect size; values that can exceed 1 (like d) keep the leading zero.

q: A clinic proposes using a general AI chatbot to analyse transcripts of (simulated) therapy sessions. Which concern should take priority?
options: Whether the chatbot writes in a friendly tone
Protecting confidential client data and keeping qualified humans responsible, since AI output can be wrong
Whether the transcripts are long enough
Whether the chatbot can produce charts
explain: Confidentiality, accuracy (including fabricated output) and human accountability are central ethical issues; AI should not be the sole basis for clinical decisions.

q: A student uses an AI tool to help draft a lab report. Which practice is most appropriate?
